paragraphs: Finding a Nash equilibrium becomes difficult when a game offers a very large set of strategies. Open-ended methods such as Policy Space Response Oracle expand the strategies under consideration as learning proceeds. This paper addresses a weakness in that process: evaluating whether a newly learned strategy actually moves the system toward equilibrium.

The authors introduce a metric called Advantage, designed around mathematical properties connected to Nash equilibrium. They establish that the metric makes each strategy update approach equilibrium. Their A-PSRO framework uses this measure to give agents a consistent learning objective across both zero-sum games, where interests directly oppose one another, and general-sum games.

Experiments report lower exploitability in zero-sum games and higher rewards in general-sum games, outperforming the algorithms evaluated. These outcomes reflect different practical goals: resisting an opponent's ability to take advantage of a strategy, and improving rewards when interests are not strictly opposed. The contribution combines a theoretically motivated measure of progress with a framework that uses it to guide strategy learning.
icml-2025-a-psro-a-unified-strategy-lear.tldr: A-PSRO uses an equilibrium-linked Advantage metric to guide strategy learning in both zero-sum and general-sum games.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning from a small labeled collection and a larger unlabeled collection when their class frequencies differ. The labeled data has a long tail: some classes appear frequently, while others have few examples. Classifiers trained for different distributions can help label the unlabeled data, but their strengths vary across samples.

The proposed method estimates whether each sample belongs to a frequent, moderately represented, or rare class, then assigns a suitable expert. That expert supplies a pseudo-label during training and a prediction during testing. The authors also show theoretically that combining experts' strengths yields a smaller bound on generalization error, supporting the use of selective assignments.

A second component combines features from multiple network depths. Deeper features distinguish classes more effectively but favor frequent classes more strongly; shallower features show the opposite trade-off. Fusing them aims to reduce this bias while retaining useful discrimination. Experiments across different settings on CIFAR-10-LT, STL-10-LT, and SVHN-LT demonstrate the method's effectiveness under the distribution mismatch it was designed to address.
icml-2025-a-square-peg-in-a-square-hole-.tldr: Dynamic expert assignment and features from multiple depths improve learning when labeled and unlabeled class distributions differ.

paragraphs: Generative recommendation predicts user actions by representing past actions as discrete tokens and generating likely continuations. Existing approaches give an action the same tokens wherever it appears. ActionPiece addresses the possibility that an action has different meanings depending on the actions around it, making its surrounding sequence relevant to tokenization itself.

Each action is represented as an unordered set of item features. ActionPiece builds a vocabulary by merging feature patterns that frequently occur together, considering both features within a single action and features across neighboring actions. Consequently, vocabulary construction can capture patterns that cross action boundaries instead of treating every action as an isolated unit.

The method also introduces set permutation regularization. Because the features form a set, changing their order preserves their meaning; the regularization uses this property to produce multiple segmentations of the same action sequence. The contribution is a context-sensitive representation procedure for generative recommendation. Its significance lies in allowing the tokens themselves to reflect relationships among actions, while accommodating equivalent orderings of their features.
icml-2025-actionpiece-contextually-token.tldr: ActionPiece builds recommendation tokens from feature patterns within and across actions so tokenization can reflect sequence context.

paragraphs: Data-driven personalized learning aims to support individual students, but the data used to develop these systems can have uneven class frequencies. The paper argues that assumptions about high-quality, well-annotated benchmarks overlook this long-tail problem. Underrepresented classes can therefore become an obstacle to the performance of personalized learning models in practical settings.

The authors propose Neural-Collapse-Advanced personalized Learning, or NCAL, which encourages learned features to follow a shared simplex equiangular tight frame structure. This is a regular geometric arrangement with equal angles between its class directions. A Text-modality Collapse regularizer shapes text embeddings within the language model's representation space toward the desired structure.

NCAL is designed to work with different architectures and existing approaches. The reported experiments show improvements to those methods, state-of-the-art performance in the evaluated settings, and better generalization alongside reduced class imbalance effects. The central idea is to address uneven representation by controlling the geometry of learned features, giving personalized learning systems a common structural target even when their training classes have unequal support.
icml-2025-advancing-personalized-learnin.tldr: NCAL regularizes text-feature geometry to reduce class imbalance effects and improve personalized learning.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language model generation, but the configuration that works well can depend on the text already produced. BanditSpec treats configuration selection as an online learning problem. It adjusts speculative decoding hyperparameters during generation without requiring model training, using feedback from the generation process to choose among available configurations.

The framework casts those choices as a multi-armed bandit problem and introduces two algorithms, UCBSpec and EXP3Spec. Their analysis uses stopping time regret to evaluate the cost of learning which configuration to select. The paper derives regret upper bounds for stochastic and adversarial reward settings, and an impossibility result establishes that UCBSpec's regret is optimal up to universal constants.

Experiments with LLaMA3 and Qwen2 report effective performance relative to existing methods. In simulated serving scenarios containing varied prompts, throughput approaches that of an oracle choosing the best hyperparameter. This empirical comparison suggests adaptive selection can recover much of the benefit of knowing the best configuration ahead of time, while the theoretical results characterize the unavoidable cost of learning that choice.
icml-2025-banditspec-adaptive-speculativ.tldr: BanditSpec learns speculative decoding configurations during generation, with regret guarantees and throughput near an oracle in simulated serving experiments.

paragraphs: Wild test-time adaptation updates a trained model for unfamiliar domains using very little incoming data under multiple shifts. Many approaches focus on deciding which samples to trust. This paper instead examines the optimization objective and finds that widely used entropy minimization produces noisy learning dynamics that substantially reduce adaptation efficiency.

The authors identify region confidence as a better alternative, shifting attention toward local regions of the embedding space. Directly optimizing this quantity is too computationally demanding for real-time use. Their method, ReCAP, models regions probabilistically so that changes in meaning within the representation space can be captured flexibly during adaptation.

ReCAP then uses a finite-to-infinite asymptotic approximation to replace the difficult region-confidence quantity with a tractable, upper-bounded proxy. This makes the regional information usable without the lengthy direct computation. Experiments report consistent improvements over existing methods across the tested datasets and wild adaptation scenarios. The findings support reconsidering what adaptation optimizes, alongside which samples it selects, when scarce and shifting data makes the update process unstable.
icml-2025-beyond-entropy-region-confiden.tldr: ReCAP replaces difficult region-confidence optimization with a tractable proxy to improve adaptation under scarce data and multiple shifts.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit learner repeatedly chooses among actions while learning their rewards. It must explore uncertain choices without accumulating too much regret, the loss from choosing suboptimal actions. This paper adds differential privacy to that problem and proposes DP-TS-UCB, a parameterized algorithm that connects Thompson Sampling with Upper Confidence Bound exploration.

The algorithm uses Gaussian priors and Gaussian differential privacy. A parameter alpha between zero and one controls its guarantees: the GDP parameter scales as T to the power 0.25(1−alpha), up to logarithmic factors, while regret is bounded by O(K log(T)^(alpha+1)/Delta). Here T is the learning horizon, K the number of actions, and Delta the suboptimality gap.

These expressions make the privacy–regret trade-off explicit: changing alpha alters the time dependence of the privacy guarantee and the logarithmic factor in regret. The proof uses Gaussian anti-concentration bounds, which characterize how probability spreads away from concentrated regions. This mathematical connection between two exploration mechanisms is also presented as a potentially useful contribution beyond the private bandit algorithm itself.
icml-2025-connecting-thompson-sampling-a.tldr: DP-TS-UCB connects two bandit exploration methods to provide an explicit, tunable trade-off between Gaussian differential privacy and regret.

paragraphs: Online decisions often depend on different summaries of uncertain outcomes, such as their average, variance, or quantiles. This paper proposes learning the whole conditional distribution so that one framework can support those different objectives. Its central challenge is regression over an infinite-dimensional function space, where the existing contextual bandit algorithms considered yield infinite regret.

The proposed regression oracle learns contextual cumulative distribution functions, which describe the probability of outcomes falling below different thresholds. It models each datum using context-dependent CDF basis functions. The analysis connects prediction error, and ultimately decision regret, to how quickly the eigenvalues of a design integral operator decrease.

For polynomial eigenvalue decay of order 1/gamma at least one, utility regret is bounded by T^((3gamma+2)/(2(gamma+2))), up to logarithmic factors. The gamma-zero case recovers the existing optimal finite-dimensional contextual bandit rate, as does exponential decay. A numerical method for computing the eigenvalue sequence supports implementation. The results explain how the complexity of learning an entire distribution translates into the quality of sequential decisions.
icml-2025-contextual-online-decision-mak.tldr: An infinite-dimensional regression framework learns contextual outcome distributions and links decision regret to eigenvalue decay.

paragraphs: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models generate samples through a sequence of computations, creating an inference bottleneck. This paper investigates a mathematical property that can help parallelize that process. Through a connection with stochastic localization, the authors prove that DDPM increments become exchangeable under an appropriate reparameterization: their joint distribution has a symmetry under reordering.

The reparameterization is central to the claim. This exchangeability result provides a route for adapting performance optimizations from autoregressive models to diffusion models with relatively little modification. As a concrete application, the authors introduce Autospeculative Decoding, which extends speculative decoding to DDPMs without requiring an additional draft model.

The theoretical analysis gives a parallel runtime speedup scaling as the cube root of K, up to logarithmic factors, relative to a sequential DDPM with K steps. A practical implementation also substantially accelerates inference across the evaluated domains. The contribution therefore connects a structural property of the generation process to an actual acceleration method, with both a runtime analysis and empirical evidence supporting its usefulness.
icml-2025-diffusion-models-are-secretly-.tldr: A reparameterized exchangeability property enables draft-free autospeculative decoding and a theoretical cube-root parallel speedup for DDPMs.

paragraphs: Understanding a diagram requires recognizing its entities and interpreting the relationships expressed by symbols, shapes, and spatial arrangements. This paper asks whether strong answers from large vision-language models actually demonstrate that ability. It separates questions about individual entities from questions about their relationships, making it possible to distinguish different sources of apparent diagram comprehension.

The authors build a test suite spanning synthetic and real diagrams from several domains. Its questions probe both recognition and reasoning, and the evaluation covers six vision-language models. The models accurately identify and reason about entities, but show notably limited ability to understand the relationships depicted between them.

Further tests indicate that much of their successful relational reasoning comes from background knowledge that provides shortcuts. A model may therefore answer a diagram question correctly without adequately interpreting the visual evidence connecting its parts. The authors conclude that the evaluated models have limited genuine diagram understanding. The study's significance is its separation of successful answers from the visual comprehension those answers might otherwise appear to establish.
icml-2025-do-vision-language-models-real.tldr: Tests of six vision-language models find strong entity understanding but weak diagram relationship understanding, often masked by background-knowledge shortcuts.

paragraphs: Researchers analyze the spectra of neural network weight matrices to assess training quality and choose settings for individual layers. One approach measures how heavy the tail of a matrix's spectral distribution is. This paper shows that matrix dimensions and aspect ratios can bias that measurement, making differences in shape look like differences in training quality.

FARMS, or Fixed-Aspect-Ratio Matrix Subsampling, addresses this by taking submatrices with a common aspect ratio. It averages their empirical spectral distributions and measures tail heaviness from that average, rather than directly from the original matrix's spectrum. This reduces the influence of matrix shape on the diagnostic signal.

The authors evaluate FARMS in image classification, scientific machine learning, and language model pruning, reporting consistently more accurate spectral analysis and more effective layer-specific hyperparameter assignment. In one LLaMA-7B pruning experiment, perplexity falls by 17.3% relative to state-of-the-art methods. That result is a particular application of the broader contribution: making spectral comparisons more informative by mitigating a geometric source of bias.
icml-2025-eigenspectrum-analysis-of-neur.tldr: FARMS uses fixed-aspect-ratio submatrices to reduce bias in spectral diagnostics and improve their use in training and pruning.

paragraphs: Multimodal protein language models combine protein sequences with structural information encoded as discrete tokens. That conversion can discard fine details and relationships in three-dimensional structures. This paper systematically examines how to improve such models, identifying both information lost during tokenization and inaccurate prediction of structure tokens as major obstacles.

The proposed design space spans generative modeling, architectures and representations that account for structure, and data exploration. Together, these choices move training toward finer-grained supervision. The approach matters because it investigates how token-based models can retain useful structural precision despite the information loss associated with converting continuous structures into discrete representations.

The reported improvements increase the diversity of generated structures and strengthen folding performance. On the PDB test set, the authors' 650-million-parameter model reduces root-mean-square deviation from 5.52 to 2.36, indicating closer agreement with reference structures. It outperforms the evaluated 3-billion-parameter baselines and matches specialized folding models in the reported comparison. These findings show that design improvements can substantially strengthen structural modeling without relying solely on a larger model.
icml-2025-elucidating-the-design-space-o.tldr: Improved supervision and structural modeling substantially strengthen a 650M protein language model's folding accuracy and generation diversity.

paragraphs: Language model servers can save computation by reusing cached key-value vectors for text repeated across requests. Conventional caching requires an exact shared prefix, which restricts reuse when an unchanged document appears after different introductory text. This situation arises in retrieval-augmented generation and few-shot learning, where reusable content can occupy different prompt contexts.

The paper formalizes position-independent caching, which allows modular reuse of these intermediate representations regardless of the preceding prefix. Its EPIC serving system introduces LegoLink to address an inappropriate attention sink at the beginning of each document. By mitigating that effect, the algorithm aims to preserve accuracy while requiring little additional computation.

Experiments report up to eightfold improvements in time to first token and sevenfold throughput gains over existing systems, with negligible or no accuracy loss. These are reported maximum gains rather than a uniform improvement for every request. The practical contribution is to expand which repeated prompt content can benefit from caching, while handling an attention behavior that could otherwise undermine the accuracy of modular reuse.
icml-2025-epic-efficient-position-indepe.tldr: EPIC reuses cached document representations across changing prefixes, reporting up to 8× faster first-token delivery with negligible or no accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations that preserve a system's governing structure, but they may be unknown in complex systems. This paper introduces LieNLSD to discover nonlinear symmetries explicitly from dynamic data. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first method that determines both the number and expressions of infinitesimal generators containing nonlinear terms.

LieNLSD starts with a library of candidate functions for infinitesimal transformations and seeks their coefficient matrix. The key theoretical result is that the corresponding prolongation formula for differential equations remains linear in those coefficients. Nonlinear candidate transformations can therefore be identified through a linear problem in the unknown parameters.

The method combines central differences from observed data with derivatives from a trained neural network, forming linear equations solved using singular value decomposition. Tests on top quark tagging and several dynamical systems show qualitative advantages over existing methods. Using the discovered symmetries to guide data augmentation improves long-rollout accuracy of neural PDE solvers by over 20%. This connects explicit mathematical discovery to better predictions over extended simulated trajectories.
icml-2025-explicit-discovery-of-nonlinea.tldr: LieNLSD discovers explicit nonlinear symmetry generators by solving linear equations and improves neural PDE forecasts through symmetry-guided augmentation.

paragraphs: Aligning language model responses with human preferences often involves learning a reward model and then updating the language model against it. Direct preference optimization simplifies that sequence by using a reparameterization that produces an implicit reward and a single training loss. This paper examines mathematical consequences of that simplification that can affect how learning behaves.

The authors prove that DPO-based objectives can have suboptimal regularization and counterintuitive interpolation behavior arising from their reparameterizations. Regularization controls how the optimization balances its objectives, so these properties concern the behavior built into the training loss itself. The analysis identifies potential pitfalls despite DPO's demonstrated success in some practical settings.

The proposed EXPO framework instead specifies explicit regularization factors without an analogous implicit-reward reparameterization. The authors prove that it satisfies desired regularization properties that prior methods do not, and experiments support both their analysis and EXPO's effectiveness. The contribution is a more transparent way to construct preference objectives, with theoretical criteria for their behavior and empirical evidence that the resulting design is useful.
icml-2025-explicit-preference-optimizati.tldr: EXPO explicitly designs preference regularization to avoid theoretical pitfalls introduced by DPO's implicit-reward reparameterization.

paragraphs: Uneven class frequencies can bias a classifier's decision boundary and reduce performance. Data-level remedies such as resampling can introduce their own problems, including losing informative examples or making errors when generating new ones. This paper explores a different intervention: deliberately adding suitably designed label noise to counteract the effect of imbalance.

The theoretical motivation comes from binary classification studies showing that appropriate label noise can move biased decision boundaries in a helpful direction. The proposed Label-Noise-based Re-balancing method, or LNR, uses an asymmetric noise model. Its design makes the noise depend on class direction rather than applying an undifferentiated corruption to all labels.

The authors report that LNR alleviates information-loss and generation-error issues associated with other data-level methods and can be combined with any classifier or algorithm-level approach. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate its superiority in the evaluated settings. The finding concerns carefully chosen noise: the useful ingredient is an intervention designed to correct imbalance, rather than a claim that arbitrary labeling mistakes improve learning.
icml-2025-learning-imbalanced-data-with-.tldr: LNR uses carefully designed asymmetric label noise to adjust biased decision boundaries and improve classification on imbalanced data.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield models store memories and retrieve them in response to queries, in a form compatible with deep learning. This paper reinterprets those operations as nonparametric regression over query-memory pairs. The perspective provides a common mathematical framework for understanding the original dense model and developing alternatives that require less computation.

The main efficient variant uses sparse structure and has subquadratic complexity. The authors establish that it retains several attractive theoretical properties of the dense model: a connection to transformer attention, convergence to fixed points, and exponential memory capacity. The efficiency change therefore comes with analysis showing that these specific properties survive.

The framework also yields linear, randomly masked, top-K, and positive random feature variants of modern Hopfield models. Experiments evaluate memory retrieval and learning tasks in synthetic and realistic settings, supporting the framework empirically. The broader contribution is a systematic route from a regression interpretation to multiple memory architectures, making computational design choices part of a unified treatment rather than a collection of unrelated modifications.
icml-2025-nonparametric-modern-hopfield-.tldr: A nonparametric regression view yields efficient Hopfield variants, including a sparse model that retains key theoretical properties.

paragraphs: Choosing a generative model by its average evaluation score assumes that one overall ranking is useful across prompts. This paper investigates a more specific choice: which model is best for the prompt currently being processed. If rankings vary with prompt type, adapting the selection can reduce queries spent on less suitable models.

PAK-UCB formulates this as a contextual bandit problem, with candidate models as actions and prompt information shared across those actions. Feedback from generated data updates kernel-based functions that predict each model's score on unseen prompts. Selection and learning proceed online, allowing the system to improve its prompt-dependent choices as it receives results.

The authors also use random Fourier features to accelerate online learning, producing RFF-UCB. Numerical experiments with real and simulated text-to-image and image-to-text models show successful identification of the best model across different sample types. The contribution concerns learning a conditional ranking: it makes the input prompt part of the selection decision instead of relying exclusively on a model's average performance.
icml-2025-pak-ucb-contextual-bandit-an-o.tldr: PAK-UCB learns prompt-dependent model selection online, with random Fourier features accelerating its score predictions.

paragraphs: Training with private data distributed across devices often uses differentially private federated learning. An alternative is to generate differentially private synthetic data for training. Existing synthetic-data methods can require carefully engineered prompts or repeated private client feedback. This paper focuses on extracting more value from that feedback by treating it as a learning signal for the generator.

The proposed POPri algorithm interprets private client feedback as a reinforcement learning reward. It uses policy optimization methods, including Direct Preference Optimization, to fine-tune language models that generate synthetic data. The aim is to improve the generated data through learned preferences rather than relying solely on prompt design and feedback-driven selection.

The authors release LargeFedBench for uncontaminated language model evaluations on federated text data. POPri closes up to 58% of the performance gap between fully private and non-private settings, compared with 28% for prior synthetic-data methods and 3% for state-of-the-art private federated learning methods. These percentages describe fractions of a performance gap closed, showing the reported benefit of optimizing the synthetic-data generator with private feedback.
icml-2025-private-federated-learning-usi.tldr: POPri turns private client feedback into preference optimization for synthetic-data generators, closing up to 58% of the private–non-private performance gap.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a language model with external information, but retrieving more material does not automatically improve its answers. Poor retrieval settings can make a system perform worse than generating without retrieved content. RAGGED provides a framework for systematically examining how retrieval components, reading models, and the amount of retrieved information interact.

The study finds that the reader's tolerance for noisy or distracting content is the key factor in stability and scalability. Some readers improve when given more retrieved material, while others deteriorate. This distinction explains why increasing retrieval depth can have opposite effects even when the overall purpose is to provide more useful evidence.

Experiments cover open-domain, multi-hop, and specialized-domain datasets. Retrievers, rerankers, and prompts affect performance, but do not fundamentally change the reader-driven trends observed. RAGGED also supplies metrics for evaluating stability and scalability. Its practical message is that retrieval depth should be assessed together with the reader's robustness, because better access to information only helps when the model can handle the accompanying distractions.
icml-2025-ragged-towards-informed-design.tldr: RAGGED finds that a reader's tolerance for distracting content largely determines whether deeper retrieval helps or harms a RAG system.

paragraphs: This paper studies language model robustness as a scaling problem: what happens when models, attackers, and defenders receive more computational resources? Across classification tasks, model families, and adversarial attacks, larger models without explicit safety training are not consistently more robust. Size alone therefore does not establish a reliable defensive advantage in the evaluated settings.

For adversarial training, larger models improve sample efficiency but worsen compute efficiency. They can learn more effectively from training examples while requiring more computation for that benefit. Meanwhile, giving attackers more compute steadily increases attack success against both undefended models and models that have undergone adversarial training.

The authors also examine how robustness transfers across attacks and threat models, then combine attack and defense scaling rates. Attack scaling outpaces adversarial training across all models studied, although the analysis suggests larger adversarially trained models might eventually favor defense. That longer-term possibility remains qualified. The contribution is a way to compare changing resource budgets, rather than treating robustness measured at one scale as a fixed property.
icml-2025-scaling-trends-in-language-mod.tldr: Robustness scaling depends on attack and defense resources, with larger models improving adversarial-training sample efficiency but not compute efficiency.

paragraphs: T1 investigates how reinforcement learning can improve language model reasoning and make additional inference computation useful. The paper argues that imitation-focused approaches struggle to scale effectively at test time, while previous reinforcement learning attempts have produced only modest improvements on difficult reasoning. Its approach emphasizes exploration during learning and examines the resulting inference behavior.

Training begins with synthesized reasoning traces that include trial and error as well as self-verification. The subsequent reinforcement learning stage uses over-sampling to encourage greater sampling diversity. These choices aim to expose the model to varied reasoning attempts and ways of checking them, rather than depending entirely on reproducing a fixed set of demonstrations.

Using open language models as starting points, T1 demonstrates inference scaling and superior performance on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The authors also introduce a simple strategy for studying that scaling: increasing the inference budget improves T1's performance without additional verification. The reported finding links the training approach to a useful deployment property, where more computation at inference can translate directly into better reasoning results.
icml-2025-t1-advancing-language-model-re.tldr: T1 encourages diverse reinforcement learning exploration and shows improved math reasoning as inference budgets increase without additional verification.

paragraphs: When agents possess private information, their actions reflect both that information and their incentives. This can create confounding, making observed behavior difficult to interpret. The paper also considers knowledge transportability: learning must draw on environments where data is available because experiments in the target environment are difficult to conduct.

The authors ask whether actions that are not independent and identically distributed can still help reveal confounders while knowledge is transferred between environments. They formulate an online strategic interaction model and develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that identifies system dynamics despite information asymmetry. The method addresses strategic behavior and transfer within the same learning problem.

The main result is a tight sample-complexity guarantee of roughly 1/epsilon squared, with logarithmic factors suppressed, for learning an epsilon-optimal policy. Such a policy comes within epsilon of optimal performance in the modeled setting. The result gives a precise account of how data requirements grow with the requested accuracy, establishing sample-efficient learning for a problem that combines hidden information, strategic actions, and knowledge transfer.
icml-2025-the-sample-complexity-of-onlin.tldr: A strategic online learning algorithm handles information asymmetry and knowledge transfer with tight sample complexity proportional to 1/epsilon² up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Robot policies need visual information about both the present scene and how it may change after an action. The paper argues that encoders trained with individual images or image pairs tend to emphasize static information. It hypothesizes that video diffusion models contain representations of current appearance alongside predicted future dynamics, making them useful for robot learning.

Video Prediction Policy, or VPP, learns an implicit inverse dynamics model conditioned on predicted future representations inside a video diffusion model. In effect, those future-oriented features help guide action learning. To improve the predictions, the authors fine-tune a pretrained video foundation model using robot datasets together with internet videos of human manipulation.

VPP achieves an 18.6% relative improvement over the previous state of the art on the Calvin ABC-D generalization benchmark. The paper also reports a 31.6% increase in success rates for complex real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. These results support the usefulness of predictive visual representations for the evaluated robot tasks, while the proposed interpretation of what video models internally represent remains the motivating hypothesis.
icml-2025-video-prediction-policy-a-gene.tldr: VPP uses predicted future representations from video diffusion models to improve robot action learning and manipulation performance.

paragraphs: RGBD simultaneous localization and mapping estimates camera motion while building a scene map from color and depth images. Gaussian-based representations support efficient rendering, but keeping every Gaussian adjustable throughout optimization creates memory and computation problems for very large scenes. VTGaussian-SLAM addresses these problems through a simpler representation and accompanying tracking and mapping strategies.

Its view-tied Gaussians are attached to depth pixels, avoiding the need to learn their positions, rotations, and multidimensional variances. This reduces storage per Gaussian and allows more Gaussians to describe local detail within the same limited GPU memory. The representation links scene elements to observed views rather than independently optimizing all of those geometric parameters.

The tracking and mapping strategies also remove the requirement to keep every Gaussian learnable throughout training. Benchmark evaluations report improvements over recent methods in rendering quality, camera tracking accuracy, and scalability. The contribution combines reduced representation cost with a different optimization strategy, showing that simplifying individual scene elements can support more detailed maps and better tracking in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-vtgaussian-slam-rgbd-slam-for-.tldr: VTGaussian-SLAM ties simplified Gaussians to depth pixels to reduce memory use and improve large-scene mapping, rendering, and tracking.
